title: Imports and Dependencies
content: Imports Mathlib's prime number basics, finite set infrastructure, natural number foundations, and tactic framework. `Nat.Prime` provides the primality predicate and `Set.Infinite`/`Set.Finite` enable stating the infinitude conjectures.
mathContext: Uses `Nat.Prime p` ($p$ is prime), `Set.Infinite S` ($|S| = \infty$), and decision procedures (`decide`, `norm_num`) for computational verification.

title: Problem Statement and Historical Context
content: Module docstring describing Erdős Problem #1065 (Guy's B46): are there infinitely many primes $p$ with $p - 1 = 2^k q$ ($q$ prime)? Lists known examples, connections to safe primes and Artin's conjecture, and the more general $2^k 3^l q + 1$ variant. References OEIS A074781 (safe primes) and A339465.
mathContext: The problem asks about the density of primes whose predecessor $p-1$ has restricted factorization. Connected to Hardy-Littlewood Conjecture F (1923) on the density of safe primes: $\pi_{\text{safe}}(x) \sim 2C_2 x/(\log x)^2$.

title: Primes of the Form $2^k \cdot q + 1$
content:
Defines the predicate `IsTwoTimePrimePlusOne p`: a prime $p$ such that $p - 1 = 2^k \cdot q$ for some prime $q$ and non-negative integer $k$. This restricts $p - 1$ to have exactly one odd prime factor. The condition means $p - 1$ is '$2$-smooth times a prime', or equivalently that $p - 1$ has at most two distinct prime factors (2 and $q$).

The $k = 1$ case ($p = 2q + 1$) gives the safe primes (see `sophie-germain`), critical in Diffie-Hellman cryptography where $p - 1$ must resist Pohlig-Hellman factoring. The Euler totient $\varphi(p) = p - 1 = 2^k q$ (see `euler-totient`) has a restricted number of divisors, making the discrete logarithm problem in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}^*$ harder when $p$ is a Form A prime.
mathContext: $\text{IsTwoTimePrimePlusOne}(p) \;:\Leftrightarrow\; p \text{ prime} \wedge \exists q, k \in \mathbb{N}: q \text{ prime} \wedge p = 2^k q + 1$. When $k = 0$, $p = q + 1$, so $p = 3, q = 2$ is the only solution. When $k = 1$, $p = 2q + 1$: these are the safe primes. The constraint $\omega(p-1) \leq 2$ (at most 2 distinct prime factors) is equivalent to the definition.

title: Primes of the Form $2^k \cdot 3^l \cdot q + 1$
content: Defines the relaxed predicate `IsTwoThreeTimePrimePlusOne p`: a prime $p$ such that $p - 1 = 2^k \cdot 3^l \cdot q$ for some prime $q$ and $k, l \geq 0$. This allows $p - 1$ to have up to three distinct prime factors. Setting $l = 0$ recovers the stronger form, so every $2^k q + 1$ prime is automatically a $2^k 3^l q + 1$ prime.
mathContext: $\text{IsTwoThreeTimePrimePlusOne}(p) \;:\Leftrightarrow\; p \text{ prime} \wedge \exists q, k, l \in \mathbb{N}: q \text{ prime} \wedge p = 2^k \cdot 3^l \cdot q + 1$. The set of such primes contains the Form A primes as $\{l = 0\} \subseteq \{l \geq 0\}$.

title: Conjecture A: Infinitely Many $2^k q + 1$ Primes
content: The stronger variant of Erdős Problem #1065: the set $\{p \text{ prime} : p - 1 = 2^k q,\; q \text{ prime}\}$ is infinite. This implies the safe primes conjecture as a special case ($k = 1$). The conjecture relates to the distribution of prime values of the polynomial $2^k q + 1$ as $q$ ranges over primes and $k$ over non-negative integers.

title: Conjecture B: Infinitely Many $2^k 3^l q + 1$ Primes
content:
The weaker variant of Problem #1065: the set of primes $p$ with $p - 1 = 2^k \cdot 3^l \cdot q$ ($q$ prime) is infinite. This is implied by Conjecture A (set $l = 0$). The extra factor of $3^l$ significantly enlarges the candidate set — for example, $p = 61$ satisfies Form B ($60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$) but not Form A.

**Why 3 is special:** The choice of 3 as the additional smooth factor is natural: the $\{2,3\}$-smooth numbers (regular numbers, studied since Babylonian mathematics) are the densest smooth number set after powers of 2. Requiring $p - 1$ to be $\{2,3\}$-smooth times a prime is the mildest relaxation of Form A's $2$-smooth condition.

title: Computationally Verified Form A Examples
content:
Proves all 14 Form A primes up to 100: $3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 23, 29, 41, 47, 53, 59, 83, 89, 97$. Each proof constructs the witness $(q, k)$ and checks primality of both $p$ and $q$ using `decide` and `norm_num`.

The pattern is uniform: `constructor` splits the conjunction into a primality check (`decide`) and an existence witness. The witness is provided as `⟨q, k, by decide, by norm_num⟩`, where `by decide` verifies primality of $q$ and `by norm_num` checks the arithmetic equation $p = 2^k \cdot q + 1$ computationally. This reflects Lean 4's strength in verified finite computation: despite the conjecture being open, the individual instances are decidable and machine-checkable in milliseconds.

title: Form B Separating Examples ($p = 37$ and $p = 61$)
content:
This section proves that $37$ and $61$ are Form B primes, establishing them as separating examples for the strict inclusion Form A $\subsetneq$ Form B.

**$p = 37$**: $36 = 2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 2$, so $(q, k, l) = (2, 1, 2)$ is a valid Form B witness. Note that $36 = 2^2 \cdot 9$ and 9 is not prime, so 37 is not Form A.

**$p = 61$**: $60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$, so $(q, k, l) = (5, 2, 1)$ is a valid Form B witness. Since $60/1 = 60$, $60/2 = 30$, $60/4 = 15$ are all composite, 61 is not Form A.

The juxtaposition of these two examples demonstrates the three-level hierarchy: {safe primes} $\subset$ {Form A} $\subset$ {Form B} $\subset$ {all primes}.
mathContext: $37 - 1 = 36 = 2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 2$: Form B witness $(q,k,l) = (2,1,2)$. $61 - 1 = 60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$: Form B witness $(q,k,l) = (5,2,1)$.
relatedConcepts: Form A vs Form B distinction

title: Non-Form-A Proof: $p = 37$
content: Proves $37$ is not Form A by exhaustive case analysis. Since $36 = 2^k \cdot q$, bounding $k \leq 4$ (as $2^5 = 32 > 36/2$) and using `interval_cases` to enumerate $k = 0, \ldots, 4$: the quotients $36, 18, 9$ are all composite, and for $k \geq 3$ the arithmetic fails via `omega`. The `not_form_a_37` section heading and docstring are included in this range.
mathContext: $37 - 1 = 36 = 2^2 \cdot 3^2$. For $k = 0$: $q = 36$ (not prime). For $k = 1$: $q = 18$ (not prime). For $k = 2$: $q = 9$ (not prime). For $k \geq 3$: $2^k \cdot q = 36$ has no solution with $q \geq 2$.

title: Non-Form-A and Non-Form-B Proofs: $p = 61$ and $p = 71$
content:
Three non-membership proofs using bounded exhaustion:

`not_form_a_61`: $60 = 2^k q$ for $k = 0,1,2$ gives $q \in \{60, 30, 15\}$, all composite. For $k \geq 3$, $2^k > 60$.

`not_form_a_71`: $70 = 2^k q$ gives $q \in \{70, 35\}$ (composite), then $2^k > 70$ for $k \geq 2$.

`not_form_b_71`: $70 = 2^k \cdot 3^l \cdot q$ is exhaustively checked over $k \leq 5, l \leq 3$ using `interval_cases k <;> interval_cases l <;> simp_all`. Since $3 \nmid 70$, only $l = 0$ cases are non-vacuous, reducing to `not_form_a_71`.
mathContext: The bounding strategy: $2^k \leq p - 1$ forces $k \leq \lfloor \log_2(p-1) \rfloor$, and $3^l \leq p - 1$ forces $l \leq \lfloor \log_3(p-1) \rfloor$. For $p = 71$: $70 = 2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7$ is $3$-free, so no factorization $2^k \cdot 3^l \cdot q$ with $q$ prime and $l > 0$ exists.

title: Strict Inclusion: Form A $\subsetneq$ Form B via Witnesses
content: `strict_inclusion_37` and `strict_inclusion_61` combine positive Form B membership with negative Form A membership to witness $\{\text{Form A}\} \subsetneq \{\text{Form B}\}$. These are the two smallest separating examples: $37 = 2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 2 + 1$ and $61 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 + 1$.
mathContext: $\text{Form A} \subsetneq \text{Form B}$ is witnessed by: $37 \in \text{Form B} \setminus \text{Form A}$ (via `example_37_extended` and `not_form_a_37`) and $61 \in \text{Form B} \setminus \text{Form A}$ (via `example_61_extended` and `not_form_a_61`).

title: Form A Implies Form B
content: Proves that every prime of the $2^k q + 1$ form is also of the $2^k 3^l q + 1$ form, by taking $l = 0$ (so $3^0 = 1$). The proof destructures the Form A hypothesis and applies the trivial embedding. This establishes the set inclusion $\{\text{Form A primes}\} \subseteq \{\text{Form B primes}\}$.

title: Connection to Sophie Germain / Safe Primes
content:
Two theorems connecting safe primes to Form A. `sophie_germain_case` proves that the infinitude of safe primes ($p = 2q + 1$ with $q$ prime) would imply Conjecture A: a safe prime is a Form A prime with $k = 1$. `safe_prime_is_form_a` provides the direct embedding. The safe primes conjecture is itself wide open — heuristically, Hardy-Littlewood Conjecture F predicts $\sim 2C_2 \cdot x / (\log x)^2$ safe primes up to $x$ where $C_2 \approx 0.66$ is the twin primes constant.

The connection to Dirichlet's theorem (see `dirichlets-theorem`) is instructive: Dirichlet proved infinitely many primes in $a + nd$ (arithmetic progressions), while this conjecture asks about primes in $2^k q + 1$ where $q$ varies over primes — a much more restrictive structured set requiring two simultaneous primality conditions.
mathContext: $\{p \in \mathbb{P} : \exists q \in \mathbb{P},\, p = 2q+1\} \subseteq \{p : \text{IsTwoTimePrimePlusOne}(p)\}$ via $k = 1$. Hardy–Littlewood predict $\pi_{\text{safe}}(x) \sim 2C_2 x/(\ln x)^2$.

title: Smooth Structure of $p - 1$
content: Extracts the factorization $p - 1 = 2^k \cdot q$ from the Form A hypothesis. The significance is that $p - 1$ is '$2$-smooth times a prime': its largest prime factor is $q$ and all other factors are powers of 2. This connects to the classical study of the factorization of $p - 1$ initiated by Artin's conjecture on primitive roots.
mathContext: $\text{IsTwoTimePrimePlusOne}(p) \implies p - 1 = 2^k q$ with $q$ prime. The number $p - 1$ is $q$-smooth with $\omega(p-1) \leq 2$.

title: Conjecture A Implies Conjecture B
content:
Proves that if the set of Form A primes is infinite, then the set of Form B primes is infinite. Uses `Set.Infinite.mono` with `form_a_implies_b` to lift the set inclusion to an infinitude implication. This formalizes the complete logical hierarchy: safe primes $\Rightarrow$ Conjecture A $\Rightarrow$ Conjecture B.

The key Mathlib lemma is `Set.Infinite.mono`: if $S \subseteq T$ and $S$ is infinite, then $T$ is infinite. The proof is essentially two lines: apply `h.mono` (where `h : Set.Infinite {Form A}`) and dispatch the subset obligation to `form_a_implies_b`.
mathContext: $|\{\text{Form A}\}| = \infty \implies |\{\text{Form B}\}| = \infty$ since $\{\text{Form A}\} \subseteq \{\text{Form B}\}$ by `form_a_implies_b`. Formally: `h.mono (fun p hp => form_a_implies_b p hp)`.

title: Decidable Check Function
content: Implements a bounded decidable check `checkTwoTimePrime p` that tests whether $p$ is of the $2^k q + 1$ form by iterating over all $k < p$ and checking if $(p-1)/2^k$ is prime. This is a brute-force algorithm but suffices for small examples. The function returns `Bool` rather than `Prop`, enabling `#eval` computation.
mathContext: Algorithm: for each $k = 0, 1, \ldots, p-1$, check if $2^k \mid (p-1)$ and $(p-1)/2^k$ is prime. Complexity: $O(p \cdot T_{\text{prime}}(p))$ where $T_{\text{prime}}$ is the cost of primality testing.

title: Collective Verification: All 14 Form A Primes $\leq 100$
content:
Proves that all 14 identified Form A primes $\leq 100$ satisfy `IsTwoTimePrimePlusOne`, packaging the individual examples into a single universally quantified statement over a list. Uses `simp [List.mem_cons]` and case splitting (`rcases`) to dispatch each element to its previously proved instance.

This is the computational evidence supporting Conjecture A: among the 25 primes up to 100, a majority (56%) have the Form A property.
